text:
Jimmy Foxx died of alcoholism
in a miserable hotel room.

Beau Jack ended up shining
shoes,
just when he was beginning.

There are dozens, hundreds,
more, perhaps a thousand more.

To be an aging athlete
is one of the cruelest
fates,
to be replaced by others,
no longer hearing the
acclaim and the experts, no longer being
recognized,
being only an old man
like any other
old man.

Almost enough not to believe
yourself,
you look through the scrapbook
with its yellowing
pages. And there you are,
smiling;
there you are,
victorious;
there you are,
young.

The crowd has other
heroes.

The crowd never
dies,
never grows old
but the crowd often
forgets
now the telephone
doesn’t ring,
the girls have
gone,
the party
is over.

That is why I chose
to be a
writer.

If you are worth a
damn thing
you can continue with
your fooling around
until the last minute
of the last
day.

You can keep
improving instead
of getting worse,
you can keep
slamming them against the
wall.

Through the darkness, the war,
with good or bad
luck
you can keep hitting them,
with the dazzling lightning
of the
word,
knocking life down in life,
and death too late to
truly win
against
you.

translation.title: Betting on the Muse
translation.editorial_note:
Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Sports names, repeated “crowd,” and the poem’s lineation are retained; capitalization is normalized for the proper names.

Imported as a translation without separate editorial review.
